newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Amplats sees Russian platinum sales drop.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Amplats sees Russian platinum sales drop.

text.p: The world's largest producer of platinum, Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd (Amplats), sees Russian supplies declining and is gearing itself to fill the supply gap.
South Africa produces 76 percent of the world's newly-mined platinum, of which about half comes from Amplats' mines in the country's NorthWest and Northern provinces.
Platinum production in Russia, the world's second-largest producer, is stable but the Russians have been selling stockpiles of the precious metal to earn much-needed foreign currency.

Amplats believed Russian platinum sales would drop to create a gap in the market, managing director Barry Davison said during an analysts' visit to the world's largest platinum mine, Rustenburg Platinum Holdings Ltd (Rusplats).

"We do expect Russian sales to decline in the medium term as a result of the depletion of their stocks and we plan to embark on certain very-cost-competitive projects in order to fill a portion of that gap that will be created as a reduction of Russian sales.
"We will obviously recognise the overall dynamics of demand and supply in order not to disrupt the market," Davison told Reuters.
Speaking during a tour of Rusplats' Union Section in the Bushveld complex -- where most of South Africa's platinum is mined -- Davison said the long-term outlook for platinum demand was good.
"The fundamentals for platinum demand over the long term are quite good," Davison said, but he noted that the weak platinum price, which had been tracking bullion closely, caused some concern.
"We are having a bit of a tough time in the industry. The gold price is dragging platinum down," he said.
Davison said Amplats would like to see platinum at around $450 and ounce.
Platinum traditionally trades at a premium to gold but in recent months it has been tracking gold which has been on a downward curve.
On Monday, platinum traded at 357.50/80 dollars an ounce against the gold price of 353.10/353.60.
Analysts said platinum was undervalued and predicted a recovery in the near future.
"The thing that needs to change is the sales of Russian stocks. But who knows how extensive they are?" said a Johannesburg analyst, who asked not to be named.
The extent of Russian platinum stocks is not known. Analysts estimate them at between two and five million ounces.
Platinum refiners Johnson Matthey said in their annual report last year that world demand was in the region of 4.79 million ounces in 1995.
Amplats' Rustenburg mines produced 1.55 million ounces in the year to June 30, 1996.
